_readme.covers: Units 28-29. Rated progressions for augmented sixth chords and Neapolitan chords.
_readme.structure: Each rule has: id, quality, from, to, feedback.

matching.from: Root numerals for the previous chord. Empty list applies only to the first chord.
matching.to: Root numerals for the current chord.
matching.bare_root: A bare numeral like 'V' matches every inversion of V.
matching.figured: A numeral with a figure like 'V65' matches only that inversion.

how_to_add_a_rule: 1. Copy a rule block between { and }.
2. Give it a new unique id.
3. Set from and to as above.
4. Pick a quality: excellent, good, fair, discouraged, bad.
6. Save. No trailing comma after the last rule.

rules.feedback: Approaching the augmented sixth from the subdominant. The 4 of the subdominant becomes the #4 of the augmented sixth, so the chromatic tone is prepared as a common tone.
Approaching the augmented sixth from the tonic. b6 and #4 are introduced chromatically, giving a striking shift of colour.
Approaching the augmented sixth from a non-subdominant harmony. Idiomatic in the nineteenth-century repertoire but unusual in strict common-practice writing.
Italian sixth resolving directly to the dominant. b6 descends to 5 and #4 ascends to 5, producing the characteristic half-step expansion into the octave on 5.
Italian sixth to the cadential 6/4. The augmented sixth interval expands by half step to the octave on 5. A standard preparation for the cadential resolution.
French sixth resolving to the dominant. Identical outer-voice resolution to the Italian sixth but with an added 2 that becomes the fifth of the dominant.
German sixth resolving to a root-position dominant. b6 descends to 5, #4 ascends to 5, and b3 is a common tone with the seventh of V⁷.
German sixth to V⁷ with the fifth of V⁷ omitted (root doubled). Necessary when moving directly to a root-position V⁷ without an intervening I⁶⁴, to avoid parallel fifths.
Augmented sixth chord resolving away from the dominant. The strong chromatic tendency tones (b6 and #4) pull outward to 5, so any other resolution contradicts the chord's function.
Approaching the Neapolitan from the tonic. The chromatic b2 enters as a chromatic alteration of the tonic's second degree, introducing a sudden shift of colour.
Approaching the Neapolitan from the subdominant family. The b6 of the previous chord can be held as a common tone, softening the chromatic shift.
Neapolitan to the dominant. The bass ascends 4 to 5, and the chromatically lowered b2 either ascends by half step to 2 (the fifth of V) or is held as an appoggiatura over V.
Neapolitan to the cadential 6/4. Bass 4 to 5 continues the standard resolution while the cadential 6/4 prepares the dominant.
Neapolitan resolving directly to tonic. The strong chromatic tension of b2 wants the dominant as a goal; arriving on the tonic directly feels premature and weakens the cadence.
Neapolitan prolonged by changing inversion. b2 is held over as a common tone rather than resolved, so the progression is a prolongation of the Neapolitan rather than a cadential approach.
Root-position Neapolitan to the dominant. b2 in the bass must resolve up to 2 (fifth of V⁶⁵) or be transferred before the dominant arrives. Less common than N⁶.
Root-position Neapolitan to tonic. b2 resolves down by step to 1, producing a chromatic plagal motion. Idiomatic in Romantic writing but unusual in strict common-practice style.
Neapolitan to an augmented sixth chord. A chromatic intensification that combines two distinctive chromatic sonorities. Common in the nineteenth-century repertoire (e.g., N⁶ → Ger⁶₅ → V).
